displayQuote: If I Could Just Make Them Up On the Spot, I'd Be Famous

meta.title: Who really said "If I Could Just Make Them Up On the Spot, I'd Be Famous"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yogi Berra really said it — to a couple at his own museum who asked him to invent a Yogi-ism on demand. He tells the story in his 2001 book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If I Could Just Make Them Up On the Spot, I'd Be Famous'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Berra. Asked to produce a Yogi-ism on request, he answered that if he could do that, he’d be famous. He tells it himself in 2001.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Berra told this one on himself. In When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It! (2001), page 138, he describes a couple at the Yogi Berra Museum asking him to say a Yogi-ism, and writes: “I told them I don’t make them up on the spot. I said if I could, I’d be famous.” Joe Posnanski recounted the same episode as direct speech in Sports Illustrated on 4 July 2011, and Quote Investigator ↗ concludes Berra coined it.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Visitors at the Yogi Berra Museum & Learning Center asking him to invent a Yogi-ism
When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It! (with Dave Kaplan), 2001, p. 138

source.excerpt: People always expect me to be funny. I guess that’s the popular image. “Make up a Yogi-ism,” they’ll say. I can’t. I don’t think I ever said anything intentionally funny in my life. Sometimes the quotes just happen—I just don’t know when I’ll say them. Once a couple visiting our museum met me and asked if I could say a Yogi-ism. I told them I don’t make them up on the spot. I said if I could, I’d be famous.
trail: Berra published the story himself in When You Come to a Fork in the Road, Take It!, written with Dave Kaplan, page 138, quoted in full by Quote Investigator ↗.

Joe Posnanski told the same episode in Sports Illustrated on 4 July 2011 with the line as direct speech: “If I could just make ’em up on the spot, I’d be famous.” The couple laughed; Berra did not know what was funny. Reproduced in Quote Investigator ↗.

Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that on Berra’s own testimony he made the statement, and that it is unlikely the words were said by someone else and later reassigned to him — the usual failure mode for Yogi-isms.

Worth knowing: many lines sold as Yogi-isms are not his, a point Berra made the subtitle of his 1998 collection The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said!. This one is on the right side of that line. It is not among the quotations documented on Wikiquote’s Berra page ↗.
source.excerptNote: From Berra’s own book, quoted in Quote Investigator ↗. Note the form: Berra reports the remark in indirect speech. The familiar direct-quotation wording — “If I could just make ’em up on the spot, I’d be famous” — comes from Joe Posnanski’s 2011 Sports Illustrated account of the same episode.

author.name: Yogi Berra
author.heading: About Yogi Berra
author.metaLine: 1925–2015 · American baseball catcher, manager and coach
author.bio: Lawrence Peter “Yogi” Berra was an American professional baseball catcher who later managed and coached, playing nineteen seasons in the major leagues, almost all of them for the New York Yankees. He became as famous for his sentences as for his catching — a reputation he regarded with some bafflement, and which attracted so many invented quotations that he titled a collection I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said!

misattribution.heading: The Yogi-ism problem
misattribution.intro: Berra is one of the most over-credited people in American quotation: lines he never said are routinely sold under his name, and he said so himself. That makes it worth stating plainly which side of the line this one falls on.

items.why: He printed the story in his own 2001 book, page 138, and the episode was independently recounted in Sports Illustrated in 2011. Quote Investigator ↗ finds good evidence he coined it.

items.who: “If I could just make ’em up on the spot”
items.why: Berra’s own book gives the remark in indirect speech (“I said if I could, I’d be famous”). The crisp direct quotation everyone repeats is Joe Posnanski’s 2011 rendering in Sports Illustrated, per Quote Investigator ↗. The substance is Berra’s; the exact phrasing is a journalist’s.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Berra — he told the story himself in 2001, and Quote Investigator ↗ finds no sign the line came from anyone else.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke is that it is not a joke. Berra was being asked to perform a kind of accidental wisdom that only works when it is accidental, and his refusal — that if he could produce them deliberately he would be famous — is itself the thing he said he could not produce. He was, of course, already famous.

It also doubles as his own account of how the Yogi-isms happened: not as material, but as ordinary sentences that turned out sideways. “I don’t think I ever said anything intentionally funny in my life,” he wrote on the same page.
detailsBody: Berra spent decades disowning quotations. His 1998 collection was subtitled I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said!, which is itself a Yogi-ism and one he did say. The museum where this exchange happened, on the Montclair State University campus in New Jersey, is named for him.
Posnanski’s 2011 telling adds the detail that makes it: the couple laughed happily, and Berra did not know what was so funny. The remark works precisely because he was not trying.
context.pull: Asked to be accidentally wise on demand, he explained why that cannot be done — and did it.
